newsitem.title: USA: What's a dollar worth? Ask the Minneapolis Fed.
newsitem.headline: What's a dollar worth? Ask the Minneapolis Fed.

text.p: You're probably making more money now than you were, say, 10 years ago. But are you really?
The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis has an online answer for you.
The bank's web site now features a revamped version of an online calculator that will adjust any dollar amount to inflation in the period between 1913 and 1997.
Just punch in the numbers and dates and the answer will flash on your screen in a few seconds.
For example: Picture a U.S. worker who had an annual salary of $30,000 in 1980.
That same American would have to be earning $58,798.54 today just to make up for the variation in retail inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) in that 17-year period.

The calculator was developed by economists and the public affairs department of the Minneapolis Fed in an effort to respond to an increasing amount of inflation-related phone calls received by the department.

"There are so many people who call us wondering what this product that they bought in 1960 or 1950 is worth in today's dollars," said Minneapolis Fed public affairs analyst Rob Grunewald, who is part of the team which developed the online calculator.
But the web site audience doesn't stop there.

Grunewald said lawyers in charge of people's estates are constantly looking for inflation-adjusted numbers to compare how much a deed or a real estate would be worth in today's dollars. Even schools are using the service.
The Minneapolis Fed analyst said he has received e-mail from teachers who said they were planning to use the site as part of their students' homework assigments.
"What I don't know is if the students are cringing or glad to have this on the Internet," Grunewald quipped.
Turning to the technical details of the site, the Minneapolis Fed analyst said the calculator does not work well in Windows 3.x or earlier Windows releases.
The program works only with Java Script-enabled browsers. Netscape browsers version 2.0 or higher will provide the best results, he said.
The database for the calculations uses the CPI for all major expenditure class items. The base-year is chained, with the 1982-1984 period equaling 100.
